hero.sub: Launched on 30 August 2026, Roman is testing image quality and calibrating its instruments before wide-field science surveys begin.

status.title: Final commissioning phase
status.sub: NASA reports successful observatory and primary-instrument checkout. The current work characterises performance through test observations before routine science.
status.updated: Checked 30 October 2026 · latest NASA status report: 22 October

commissioning.title: Science commissioning begins
commissioning.body: The observatory can point, take exposures and transmit data. Teams are now refining image quality and measuring instrument response through planned test observations.

focus.title: WFI checkout and optical alignment
focus.body: Engineers tested the detectors, filters, internal calibration lights and thermal controls, then refined the telescope’s optical alignment. These checks prepare WFI for consistent survey measurements.

card.fovFoot: About 100 times the image area of Hubble’s ACS/WFC; not 100 times its resolution
card.lifespanFoot: Five-year primary mission. A fuel-lifetime estimate does not guarantee an equally long operating mission.

surveys.title: Three surveys, three ways to study the Universe
surveys.intro: WFI’s core surveys connect wide sky coverage with repeated measurements.

items.title: High-Latitude Wide-Area Survey
items.body: Weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering will probe matter distribution and the history of cosmic expansion.

items.title: High-Latitude Time-Domain Survey
items.body: Repeated visits will track supernovae and other changing sources, providing another route to study expansion.

items.title: Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey
items.body: Monitoring dense star fields will reveal temporary magnifications caused by intervening objects, including planetary systems.

surveys.note: These are planned observing programmes. Their goals are not already completed discoveries.

instruments.wfi_body: WFI combines 18 infrared detectors into an approximately 300-megapixel focal plane for imaging and spectroscopy. October checkout covered the instrument and optical alignment; calibration continues during science commissioning.
instruments.cgi_body: The Coronagraph Instrument suppresses starlight to test direct imaging of giant planets and dust disks. It is a technology demonstration for future observatories, not an Earth-like-planet imaging survey.

l2.description: Illustration of the Sun, Earth and Roman’s target halo orbit around Sun–Earth L2
l2.note: Schematic, not to scale; no current spacecraft position is shown. A halo orbit needs periodic corrections. Near L2, the observatory moves around the Sun with Earth while keeping sunlight away from its optics.

items.question: Are test images already the science survey?
items.answer: No. Test exposures establish instrument performance. NASA’s 25 September update anticipated science operations by early 2027; that is a published expectation, not a guaranteed image-release date.

items.question: Does 100 times the view mean 100 times sharper?
items.answer: It refers to the area covered in an image compared with a Hubble camera. Wider coverage and finer resolution describe different capabilities; surveys also depend on filters, exposure and observing strategy.

items.question: Will Roman photograph another Earth?
items.answer: Its microlensing survey detects planets through changes in background starlight. The separate coronagraph demonstrates direct-imaging technology for giant planets and disks. Neither goal promises an image of an Earth twin.

iconic.note: These are ground preparation photographs, not Roman’s astronomical observations.

orbit.sub: Roman is travelling toward Sun–Earth L2, around 1.5 million km from Earth. NASA’s 14 September trajectory update targets orbital insertion in early December 2026.

news.error: Mission news is temporarily unavailable. The dated NASA status reports above remain available.

items.question: Are the colours what an eye would see?
items.answer: Images combine exposures through selected filters. Colour can represent visible light, other wavelengths or chemical features; the caption explains the mapping.

items.question: Does Hubble magnify a single photograph?
items.answer: An observation has a chosen field, filter and exposure. Detailed release images may combine many observations, rather than being a single camera snapshot.

items.question: Did Webb replace Hubble?
items.answer: No. Hubble’s ultraviolet and visible observations complement Webb’s infrared work. Comparing wavelengths can reveal different physical components of the same object.

science.sci1_body: Hubble improved distances to galaxies and estimates of the expansion rate. The Universe’s age is inferred using these and other measurements within cosmological models.
science.sci3_body: Spectra and images help infer compact central masses from surrounding stars and gas, providing evidence for supermassive black holes.

future.title: Operations and orbital lifetime
future.decayBody: Atmospheric drag lowers the orbit. NASA’s 30 October 2026 analysis places likely re-entry in 2033–2034 without intervention; the timing depends on the evolving orbit and atmosphere.
future.proposalBody: On 30 October 2026 NASA issued a request for information on commercial servicing and an orbit boost. It is a study of options, not an approved servicing flight.

card.orbitFoot: Low Earth orbit; altitude changes with drag and time

orbit.sub: Hubble orbits Earth above most of the atmosphere. This diagram explains the orbital geometry; its scale and marker do not provide a live position or altitude.

items.question: Why do infrared images have visible colours?
items.answer: Webb measures infrared light, which our eyes cannot see. Image processors assign visible colours to filters to show structures and wavelength differences.

items.question: Does an atmospheric molecule prove life?
items.answer: No. A spectral feature needs careful identification and a physical explanation. Atmospheric composition alone does not establish biology.

items.question: Why use a halo orbit near L2?
items.answer: It helps keep the Sun, Earth and Moon on the shielded side. The observatory orbits the Sun with Earth and needs corrections to remain near L2.

l2.intro: Webb follows a halo orbit near Sun–Earth L2, moving around the Sun with Earth. The sunshield keeps the Sun, Earth and Moon on its warm side; periodic manoeuvres maintain the orbit.
l2.servicing_body: No Hubble-style astronaut servicing capability was built into Webb.

science.sci1_body: Spectra help confirm distances to early galaxies. A candidate identified from image colours needs further checks before receiving a secure distance.
science.sci3_body: Measurements of early galaxies’ abundance, brightness and composition constrain how galaxies formed. Interpretation evolves as samples and models improve.

items.question: What does touching the Sun mean?
items.answer: Parker crosses regions of the corona, the Sun’s outer atmosphere. It does not land on the visible surface.

items.question: Why approach so closely?
items.answer: Local measurements of particles and fields connect solar-wind behaviour with the environment where it originates, complementing remote images.

items.question: Does the heat shield protect every instrument?
items.answer: The shield protects most systems, while selected instrument components face the solar environment. Thermal design and spacecraft pointing are both essential.

s1.eyebrow: Calculated distances · latest available API data

voyager.dataUnavailable: Current estimates are unavailable. Historical reference distances are not substituted for live data.

rtg.v1Body: RTGs convert heat from radioactive decay into electricity. Available electrical output falls by about 4 watts each year; the team prioritises instruments and heaters.
rtg.v2Body: The spacecraft has the same long-term power constraint. Instrument shutdown decisions extend useful operation; a fixed battery percentage cannot describe this process.

voyager.powerNote: Science lifetime depends on power and equipment health, not a guaranteed retirement date.
